title: Bach and Baroque music
subject: art
description: Johann Sebastian Bach, cantor at Leipzig, pushed the fugue and counterpoint to their highest point and became the architect of the Baroque.

hero.hook: A cantor in Leipzig built the West's cathedral of sound.

blocks.text: **Johann Sebastian Bach** (**1685**-**1750**) is often called the summit of Western music. An architect of sound, he brought the art of the **fugue** and of [[Counterpoint]] to perfection: several independent melodic lines woven together.
His was not the life of a court star. It was the life of a craftsman of genius, working for the Church and for princes, whose music would only be fully rediscovered in the 19th century.

sections.title: The Baroque: church, court, and stage

blocks.text: The **Baroque** era ran from about **1600** to Bach's death. It loved contrast, movement, and ornament. **Vivaldi** in Italy and **Handel** in Germany and then England dominated the scene. Music served three masters: the church (organ and sacred song), the chamber of princes, and the stage (opera).

Bach wrote no opera, but he poured its drama into his Passions and oratorios. He fused French measure, Italian lyricism, and German rigor. For him, music mirrored a divine order, not merely a pleasant sound.
In 1717, at Weimar, Bach spent a month in jail for pressing too hard to resign: the duke would not let him leave for Köthen.

sections.title: Leipzig: the cantor and his cantatas

blocks.text: Born at **Eisenach** in **1685** into a dynasty of musicians, Bach settled in **1723** at **Leipzig** as [[cantor]] of St. Thomas Church. The workload was crushing: a new [[cantata]] almost every week, plus teaching at the [[Thomasschule]].

blocks.caption: Bach, heir to a line of German musicians
St. Thomas in Leipzig: the daily round of cantor Bach

blocks.text: He is thought to have written about **300** cantatas, and some **200** have survived. He had **20** children from two marriages. **Carl Philipp Emanuel** and **Johann Christian** became major composers themselves. In the evenings he directed the [[Collegium Musicum]], an ensemble for which he wrote concertos and secular suites.
Late in life, after eye surgery by the traveling surgeon John Taylor, Bach went blind shortly before he died.

sections.title: The Well-Tempered Clavier and the rediscovery

blocks.text: With [[Equal temperament]], a tuning system that evens out the intervals, Bach proved that one keyboard could play in every key. *The Well-Tempered Clavier* (48 preludes and fugues) opened the road to modern music. In his fugues a single theme is taken up by voice after voice: architecture built out of mathematics.

blocks.caption: The Well-Tempered Clavier: every key on one keyboard

blocks.text: After his death, fashion turned to the lighter [[style galant]]. Bach sounded “Gothic.” In **1829**, the young **Felix Mendelssohn** conducted the *St. Matthew Passion* in Berlin: the start of the “Bach revival.” Without him, hundreds of scores might have vanished.
Mendelssohn joked that it took a converted Jew and an actor, his friend Devrient, to give the world back the greatest masterpiece of Christian music.

sections.title: SDG, Voyager, and a universal legacy

blocks.text: A devout Lutheran, Bach often signed **SDG** (*Soli Deo Gloria*, glory to God alone). He played with [[numerology]] and coded his own name, B-A-C-H, into notes. In **1977**, NASA placed several of his works on the [[Golden Record]] carried by the Voyager probes, a sound embassy from humanity to space.
